allOf.description: Inherits shared step-base properties ($schema, id, owner, created_at, canonical_refs_used).

fixtures.description: Array of test fixtures providing concrete input/expected pairs for validating spec artifacts. Each fixture must reference at least one spec artifact and provide verifiable input/output pairs. A fixture typically validates one acceptance criterion from an FR and one API contract simultaneously. Example: fix-auth-login-success validates ac-login-success from fr-user-login AND the success response contract for api-auth-login. Anti-pattern: fixtures that target only an FR without also targeting the corresponding API contract when one exists.

items.description: A single test fixture with input data, expected output, testing mode, and target references. Fixtures are the executable contracts between spec and implementation.

fixture_id.description: Unique kebab-case identifier for this fixture. Naming convention: fix-{feature}-{scenario}-{mode-suffix-optional}. Examples: 'fix-auth-login-success' (happy path unit test), 'fix-auth-login-invalid-e2e' (end-to-end invalid credentials test), 'fix-payment-duplicate-redteam' (adversarial duplicate payment test). Should be stable across spec versions — renaming breaks traceability links. Anti-pattern: 'fix-1', 'fix-test-001' (sequential labels with no traceable meaning).

description.description: Human-readable description of what this fixture tests. Format: 'Given [precondition], when [action], then [expected outcome].' Example: 'Given a user account with email alice@example.com exists and email_verified=true, when POST /auth/login is called with correct credentials, then a 200 response with a JWT token is returned within 200ms.' Alternative format: '{fr-id or target}: {scenario} → {expected outcome}'. Examples: 'fr-user-login: valid credentials submitted → 200 OK with session_token in response body', 'api-payment-charge: amount exceeds account balance → 422 INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS error with retry guidance'. Anti-pattern: 'Tests login' (no precondition, action, or expected outcome); 'FR-03 login test' — use the kebab-case fr-id format (not FR-03 number format) and include the expected outcome.

targets.description: Array of spec artifact references that this fixture validates. Include all artifacts this fixture provides evidence for. Decision rule: list both the FR (behavioral correctness) and the API (contract compliance) when a fixture covers both. Example targets array: [{"id": "fr-user-login", "type": "fr", "note": "validates: FR acceptance criterion"}, {"id": "api-auth-login", "type": "api", "note": "validates: API contract"}]. type = the canonical kind of the target (fr, api, nfr, invariant); the validates relationship goes in note. Both the FR acceptance criterion and the API contract are validated by the same fixture. Validated artifacts must exist in the upstream spec files — a missing target ID causes fixtures-lint to fail. Anti-pattern: targeting only the FR without the corresponding API contract. Valid target ID types: fr-* (functional requirement from Step 04), api-* (API contract from Step 05), nfr-* (non-functional requirement from Step 07), inv-* (invariant from Step 06). Each fixture must target at least one artifact. Target at least one FR and one API when the fixture validates an HTTP endpoint — this ensures both the requirement and the contract are covered. Anti-pattern: targeting only the FR without the corresponding API contract, or fabricating a target ID that does not exist in the spec.

items.description: A trace reference to a spec artifact this fixture validates. At step 08, type = the canonical kind of the validated target: use type='fr' for fr-* IDs, type='api' for api-* IDs, type='nfr' for nfr-* IDs, type='invariant' for inv-* IDs. The validates relationship goes in note. Example: {"type": "fr", "id": "fr-user-login", "note": "validates: happy path — valid credentials return session token"}. Anti-pattern: type='validates' — 'validates' is a relationship verb, not a canonical kind; use the target's kind instead. Anti-pattern: pointing to a cap-* ID — fixtures target FRs and APIs, not capabilities directly.

mode.description: Testing mode that determines how this fixture is executed. Decision rules: 'unit' — test a single function or validation rule in complete isolation with all dependencies mocked, no network calls; 'contract' — test the request/response boundary at the API layer, service dependencies mocked but the HTTP handler is live (use for api-* targets); 'e2e' — test a full user journey across integrated components where the service layer is real (use for fr-* targets that span multiple components); 'redteam' — adversarial inputs designed to trigger security, data-integrity, or business-logic violations. For fr-user-login: unit mode tests the JWT signing logic in isolation (all HTTP mocked); contract mode tests the POST /auth/login endpoint with auth service mocked; e2e mode tests the full login flow including DB and session store; redteam mode tests alg:none JWT attack and SQL injection in the email field. Anti-pattern: using 'unit' for fixtures that reference an api-* target — those should be 'contract' or 'e2e'.

input.description: The input data used to set up this fixture's test scenario. Should be concrete and realistic — use representative values that reflect actual production data shapes. Include: required fields, boundary values, and any data that triggers the specific behavior being tested. Good: {"email": "alice@example.com", "password": "hunter2"} (real-looking, domain-specific). Bad: {"email": "test", "password": "test"} (not representative of real data) or {"data": {...}} (wrapped in unnecessary envelope). Use realistic but non-PII data. Avoid: generic placeholder values ('foo', 'test123'), incomplete objects, or data that doesn't reflect the real system's constraints.

expected.description: The expected system behavior after applying the input. Each outcome should be: (1) specific — reference exact field names, status codes, or system states; (2) verifiable — an engineer should be able to write an assertion from this; (3) complete — cover all observable effects of the operation. Example: 'Response status 201, response body contains user_id and auth_token, database record created with correct email hash'.

tags.description: Array of short labels for categorising and filtering fixtures in CI. At least one tag recommended. Standard tags to consider: 'smoke' (run on every commit), 'regression' (run on PR), 'performance' (load/stress tests), 'security' (auth/authz coverage), 'slow' (tests that take >5s). Example: ["auth", "critical", "pii"]. CI pipeline runs --tags critical for pre-merge gates and --tags auth for auth-service-specific test suites. Each tag must match the pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,64}$. Anti-pattern: more than 5 tags per fixture — over-tagging reduces the value of tag-based filtering. Anti-pattern: custom tags that are never filtered on in CI — tags only add value when pipeline configuration uses them.

items.description: A short categorisation label. Use lowercase letters, digits, dots, colons, and hyphens only. Examples: 'smoke', 'regression', 'security', 'slow', 'env:prod-only', 'fr:user-login'. Colon-separated tags (env:, fr:) create namespaced categories. Anti-pattern: spaces or uppercase (use dots/colons as separators, not spaces); avoid tags longer than 20 characters.

tag_ref.description: Canonical reference to a tag defined in the canonical registry. Required for every fixture. Kind is structurally pinned to 'tag'. Example: {"id": "cn:core:tag:critical-path", "kind": "tag", "label": "critical-path"}. Always populate tag_ref with the primary canonical tag for this fixture. If the appropriate tag is not yet in the canon registry, add it there first using 'specdev canon-accept' before authoring this fixture.
